ZIYI WU · RESEARCH IN HUMAN–ENVIRONMENT RELATIONSHIPS

Tracing connections between people, places, and nature.

Hi, I'm Ziyi Wu, a first-year master's student at the Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

I'm curious about how ecosystems, human activities, and human well-being are connected across spatial and social contexts. With a background in geography and environmental science, I enjoy exploring meaningful research questions, developing my own ideas, and finding ways to investigate them.

Feel free to reach out at wuziyi26@mails.ucas.ac.cn.

01 / A little more about me

About Me

I come from Shanxi, China, and studied Resources and Environmental Science at Beijing Normal University. I am now a first-year master's student at the Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

My interest in research began during my second year of undergraduate study, when I was introduced to ecosystem services research. As I read more papers, I gradually developed my own understanding of the field. In 2025, I joined Professor Fei Li's research group, where I began formulating my own research questions and exploring ways to investigate them, drawing on both my academic training and methods I learned independently.

One of my favorite parts of research is discovering how new ideas from the literature connect with, challenge, and reshape what I thought I knew. I enjoy developing hypotheses, testing them against evidence, and revising them when reality turns out to be more complicated than expected. For me, the excitement of research lies not only in finding answers, but also in discovering better questions.

As I use data and analytical tools to understand the world, the world continually reshapes how I understand it.

Looking ahead, I hope to better understand ecosystem dynamics and services in human-modified landscapes, drawing on both ecological and social perspectives to explore the complexity of human–environment relationships.

Research / 01 · Mongolian Plateau

When Ecosystems Meet Human Well-Being: Why Context Matters

Spatial and temporal relationships across the Mongolian Plateau
Oct 2025 – Sep 2026  ·  Lead Researcher & First Author  ·  Supervisor: Fei Li
Manuscript under review at Journal of Cleaner Production

Beyond the Space–Time Distinction

Places with richer ecosystem services may also exhibit higher human well-being. But does this mean that changes in ecosystem services within a region will necessarily be accompanied by similar changes in well-being over time?

Not necessarily.

Previous research has highlighted differences between spatial and temporal ecosystem service–human well-being (ES–HWB) associations. Yet these differences raise another question:

Does the divergence between spatial and temporal relationships itself depend on the social–ecological contexts in which people live?

We explored this question by examining whether national and livelihood contexts distinguish different ES–HWB relationships in different ways.

Why the Mongolian Plateau?

The Mongolian Plateau offers a compelling setting for this investigation.

Inner Mongolia of China and Mongolia share a broadly continuous grassland landscape, yet differ in national institutions, development trajectories, and approaches to resource governance. Across the region, pastoral areas and agro-pastoral ecotones also represent contrasting livelihood and land-use settings.

These contrasts allow us to examine ES–HWB relationships along two dimensions of social–ecological context: national setting and livelihood setting.

How We Investigated It

We examined five ecosystem services, three dimensions of human well-being, and an overall well-being index across 34 administrative regions of the Mongolian Plateau from 2001 to 2020.

Rather than treating spatial and temporal relationships as interchangeable, we examined them separately:

  • Temporal associations: How ecosystem services and human well-being varied together within each region over time.
  • Spatial associations: How ecosystem services and human well-being were associated across regions within each year.

We then investigated how the divergence between these two types of associations differed across national and livelihood groups.

To synthesize these comparisons, we developed a two-dimensional diagnostic framework describing the relative strengths of national- and livelihood-related differentiation.

Different Relationships, Different Contexts

Our central finding is that contextual differentiation is not uniform across ecosystem service–human well-being relationships.

For example, the temporal–spatial divergence in the association between forage production and material well-being differed more strongly across livelihood groups. By contrast, the divergence in the habitat quality–overall well-being association differed more strongly across national groups.

Across the 20 ES–HWB relationships examined, 15 exhibited significant temporal–spatial differences after false discovery rate correction, while 10 of these also had 95% two-way bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero.

Our two-dimensional framework illustrates how different relationships occupy different positions along national- and livelihood-related contextual gradients.

Importantly, these positions are better understood as continuous differences rather than fixed categories. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the relative strengths of contextual differentiation were generally more stable than assignments to discrete diagnostic regions.

Why Context Matters

Our findings highlight two considerations for understanding the connections between ecosystems and human well-being.

First, relationships observed across places should not automatically be interpreted as expectations for changes over time.

Second, ES–HWB relationships may not transfer unchanged across different social–ecological contexts. Their interpretation requires attention not only to analytical scale and dimension, but also to the settings in which they are observed.

This study provides a diagnostic account of associations rather than causal evidence that national institutions or livelihood systems produced the observed differences. Understanding the mechanisms behind these contextual patterns remains an important direction for future research.

Research status: Manuscript under peer review. Findings and interpretations may be revised.

Research / 02 · China–Russia Border Region

Beyond the Mine: Rethinking How We Represent Coal Mining Landscapes

Industrial systems and vegetation patterns along the China–Russia border
Sep 2026–Present  ·  Master's Research Project  ·  Supervisor: Fei Li
Ongoing research

Looking Beyond the Mine

A coal mine is more than an extraction site.

Beyond the mining area, coal production involves processing facilities, transportation terminals, and the corridors connecting them. Together, these components form an industrial system that extends across the landscape.

Yet when examining the environmental surroundings of mining activities, spatial analyses often begin with a much simpler measure: distance from the mine.

This raises a question:

What might we overlook when we represent a coal mining system only by its extraction site?

My research explores whether incorporating the wider industrial system can provide additional information about surrounding vegetation patterns, beyond what conventional mine-centric representations capture.

Why the China–Russia Border Region?

The China–Russia border region offers a setting where coal mining systems intersect with diverse ecological landscapes.

Across the study area, mining and transportation infrastructure coexist with grasslands, forests, rivers, and other land-cover types. The spatial organization of industrial facilities and transport routes provides an opportunity to examine how different components of a mining system relate to surrounding vegetation conditions.

Rather than treating each mine as an isolated location, I examine how its connected industrial facilities can be represented within a broader geographical setting.

How I Investigated It

I developed a spatial representation of 24 coal mining systems across the China–Russia border region, incorporating four components:

  • Mine: Extraction areas.
  • Processing: Coal processing facilities.
  • Terminal: Transportation and transfer terminals.
  • Edge: Transportation corridors connecting industrial components.

Using satellite-derived vegetation data from 2015, 2020, and 2025, I examined how these different spatial components were associated with surrounding vegetation patterns, primarily measured by the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI).

The analysis integrated environmental covariates, generalized additive models, multi-scale comparisons, spatial cross-validation, conditional spatial matching, and bootstrap uncertainty assessment.

By comparing models with different combinations of industrial-system components, I evaluated whether moving beyond mine-centric distances could improve the representation and prediction of vegetation patterns.

What I Found

The spatial representation of a mining system matters for how we model its surrounding vegetation.

In spatial cross-validation using the 2025 data, the full industrial-system model reduced out-of-sample NDVI prediction error by approximately 9.8% compared with the mine-centric model.

Importantly, the added information was not distributed equally across industrial components. Incorporating processing facilities and transportation terminals provided substantial improvements in prediction, suggesting that these locations contain spatial information not fully captured by distance to the mine alone.

Additional analyses also identified vegetation differences associated with transportation-corridor proximity under comparable conditions of distance to industrial nodes and selected environmental characteristics.

Beyond vegetation prediction, the more complete industrial-system representation improved precision and reduced false positives in preliminary low-NDVI screening.

Together, these findings suggest that representing mining as a connected industrial system can provide a more informative basis for examining vegetation patterns than considering extraction sites alone.

Why It Matters

A mine-centric perspective emphasizes the extraction site as the primary spatial reference. However, the geography of coal production extends beyond that site through processing facilities, transportation terminals, and connecting infrastructure.

My findings suggest that how we define the spatial structure of an industrial system can influence the ecological patterns we identify and the performance of models used to examine them.

This offers a starting point for developing more system-oriented approaches to ecological spatial assessment in resource-based industrial landscapes.

The current results concern spatial associations and predictive performance, rather than causal estimates of environmental impacts from mining activities. The research is ongoing, and the interpretation of these patterns remains subject to further evaluation.

Looking Ahead

This study forms an initial component of my broader master's research on coal industrial systems and ecological environments.

Building on the spatial representation developed here, I hope to explore how industrial organization, resource flows, and ecological conditions can be examined together. Future work may incorporate perspectives from industrial ecology, economic geography, and related social sciences to better understand resource-based industrial systems and their implications for sustainable regional development.

Research status: Ongoing research. Findings and interpretations are preliminary and may be refined as the study progresses.
